title: Temptation and Calling
overview: Matthew Chapter 4 presents a pivotal moment in Jesus’ earthly ministry, beginning with His testing in the wilderness and culminating in the calling of His first disciples. After fasting for forty days, Jesus faces direct temptations from Satan, which He overcomes by quoting Scripture, demonstrating His obedience and reliance on God’s word. Following this, Jesus begins His public ministry in Galilee, preaching repentance and the nearness of the kingdom of heaven. He calls Simon Peter, Andrew, James, and John to follow Him, promising to make them 'fishers of men.' The chapter closes with Jesus teaching, preaching, and healing throughout Galilee, attracting great crowds. This chapter sets the tone for Jesus’ mission and reveals His authority over temptation, His fulfillment of prophecy, and His invitation to discipleship.
structure:
**Verses 1-11: The Temptation of Jesus.** Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness where He fasts for forty days and nights. Satan tempts Him three times, each temptation met with a scriptural rebuke, affirming Jesus’ divine sonship and obedience to God’s word.

**Verses 12-17: Jesus Begins His Galilean Ministry.** Upon hearing of John the Baptist’s imprisonment, Jesus moves to Galilee, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy about the light dawning in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. He begins preaching a message of repentance because the kingdom of heaven is near.

**Verses 18-22: The Calling of the First Disciples.** Jesus calls Simon Peter and Andrew, then James and John, all fishermen, to follow Him and become 'fishers of men.' They immediately leave their livelihoods and families to follow Him.

**Verses 23-25: Jesus’ Ministry of Teaching, Preaching, and Healing.** Jesus travels throughout Galilee, teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing various diseases and afflictions. His fame spreads, and large crowds follow Him from diverse regions.

keyVerses.text: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights Jesus’ reliance on Scripture as the ultimate source of life and sustenance, emphasizing spiritual nourishment over physical needs. It sets a pattern for resisting temptation through God’s word.

keyVerses.text: Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.
keyVerses.significance: Here Jesus firmly rejects Satan’s offer, affirming exclusive worship and service to God alone. This underscores the centrality of worship in the believer’s life and Jesus’ authority over evil.

keyVerses.text: From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
keyVerses.significance: This verse marks the inauguration of Jesus’ public ministry and introduces the core message of repentance in light of the imminent kingdom of heaven, calling people to spiritual renewal.

keyVerses.text: And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
keyVerses.significance: Jesus’ call to the disciples signifies the beginning of their transformation and mission. It illustrates the call to discipleship and evangelism central to Christian life.

characters.name: Jesus Christ
characters.description: The Son of God who is led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted. He resists Satan’s temptations through Scripture, begins His public ministry, calls His first disciples, and ministers through teaching, preaching, and healing.

characters.name: Satan (the devil)
characters.description: The tempter who challenges Jesus in the wilderness with three specific temptations aimed at undermining His mission and identity. He ultimately fails and departs, demonstrating Jesus’ victory over evil.

characters.name: Simon Peter and Andrew
characters.description: Two brothers and fishermen whom Jesus calls to leave their nets and follow Him. They respond immediately, symbolizing the call to discipleship and the beginning of Jesus’ inner circle.

characters.name: James and John
characters.description: Brothers and sons of Zebedee, also fishermen, called by Jesus to follow Him. They leave their father and livelihood, illustrating total commitment to Jesus’ mission.

themes.description: This chapter vividly portrays Jesus’ confrontation with Satan’s temptations and His victory through Scripture, setting a model for believers to resist sin and trust God’s word.
Jesus’ preaching of repentance because the kingdom of heaven is near introduces the central theme of God’s reign breaking into history, inviting a response of faith and transformation.
The immediate response of the fishermen to Jesus’ call highlights the cost and commitment of following Christ, emphasizing the call to participate in His mission.
Jesus’ move to Galilee fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy about a great light shining in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, affirming His messianic identity and divine plan.
Jesus’ ministry of healing demonstrates His authority over sickness and evil, revealing God’s compassion and the in-breaking of the kingdom’s restorative power.

historicalContext: Matthew 4 is set in the early first century AD during the Roman occupation of Palestine. The wilderness where Jesus is tempted was a harsh, desolate region symbolizing testing and purification. Galilee, where Jesus begins His ministry, was a diverse and somewhat marginalized region known as 'Galilee of the Gentiles,' reflecting a mixed population and cultural influences. The political climate was tense, with Roman authority and Jewish expectations of a Messiah creating anticipation and unrest. John the Baptist’s imprisonment by Herod Antipas marks the dangerous political environment surrounding Jesus’ ministry. Jewish customs such as fasting, synagogue teaching, and prophetic fulfillment shaped the religious context in which Jesus operated.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes Jesus’ perfect obedience during temptation as the fulfillment of the covenant and the model for believers. The call to repentance and the proclamation of the kingdom highlight God’s sovereign grace and the necessity of faith.

Dispensationalists see the temptations as a test of Jesus’ messianic role and the beginning of His earthly ministry distinct from the church age. The fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy is viewed as a literal fulfillment pointing to Israel’s restoration.

Early Church Fathers, such as Augustine and Chrysostom, interpreted the wilderness temptation as Christ’s victory over sin and the devil, affirming His divine nature and humanity. They also stressed the importance of Scripture in spiritual warfare and the call to holiness.

crossReferences.connection: Parallel account of Jesus’ temptation in the wilderness, providing additional details and confirming the significance of this event.
Prophecy about the land of Zebulun and Naphtali seeing a great light, fulfilled by Jesus’ ministry in Galilee.
Scripture Jesus quotes in response to Satan’s temptation about man living by every word of God.
The passage Satan misuses to tempt Jesus to throw Himself down, illustrating the misuse of Scripture.
Another account of Jesus calling His first disciples, highlighting their immediate response.
Parallel narrative of Jesus beginning His ministry and calling the first disciples.

application: Use Scripture as your primary defense against temptation, memorizing and meditating on God’s word.
Recognize the importance of repentance as the first step in entering God’s kingdom and maintaining fellowship with Him.
Respond immediately and obediently to Jesus’ call in your life, trusting Him to transform your purpose.
Embrace the reality of spiritual warfare but stand firm in the authority of Christ over evil.
Follow Jesus’ example of ministry by combining teaching, preaching, and compassionate service to others.
Trust God’s promises and providence even in times of testing and uncertainty.
conclusion: Matthew 4 powerfully introduces the nature of Jesus’ ministry through His victory over temptation, His fulfillment of prophecy, and His call to discipleship. It challenges believers to rely on Scripture, repent, and follow Christ wholeheartedly. The chapter’s themes of spiritual warfare, kingdom proclamation, and healing ministry remain foundational for Christian faith and practice, encouraging believers to live in obedience and confidence in Jesus’ authority and mission.
timeline: c. AD 27-28 - Beginning of Jesus’ public ministry

definitions.definition: To be enticed or tested, especially by Satan, to sin or disobey God.
To turn away from sin and turn toward God with a changed heart and mind.
The reign and rule of God, both a present spiritual reality and a future consummation.
The highest point or peak, here referring to the top of the temple in Jerusalem.
A metaphor used by Jesus to describe the mission of His disciples to gather people into God’s kingdom.
